item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Having been through the whole extended, classic creepypasta circuit when I was in my early-to-mid-teens — joining creepypasta groups on social media; watching and reading copious amounts of creepypasta series; hunting down creepy images to imagine what stories might exist about them; needing to feel scared over again in more bizarre and terrifying ways; and at a point, even creating my own creepypasta community page for sharing and posting memes and art — I admire the care that went into this.

+ Show Commentary & Critique
– hide block

There's a lot to say about this niche of internet culture that, honestly, still thrives into this day. Yet it has remained out of mainstream attention. Obviously, this makes sense; a wider audience will not laud stories — about supernatural psycho-killers and science experiments gone wrong which gravely scar children — for their subject matter. I'm glad you've taken this niche and carved out a place for it on the modern Wiki. I wish more works could hearken back to this age of the internet in authentic ways.

I don't read much Parawatch. And while my teenage creepypasta journey always led me back to roleplay forums about conspiracies and the supernatural (like /x/), what felt most gripping was the novel experience of reading something clearly fictional which still haunted me hours after. But it's the latter that Parawatch articles often neglect to focus on, when that's what was predominant in this niche during that time.

I guess, then, to get into the issue I had with this piece, it's that it is authentic. This Parawatch user's story about his creepypasta murderer is indicative of the plethora of often cast-out and neglected creepypasta works that were put out at the time. And that's not all bad — as a kid, there is always something so charming in contributing these creepy stories, and wanting to reach back and find more.

But this article transcends that; this article says no, the kid's story is real, and somehow, reality shifts to accommodate. And like in those early creepypastas, in looking back, I find that immensely difficult to accept. Obviously, this is fiction, but it almost betrays the logic typically followed in these stories. Of toeing the line between what is constructed, and what isn't. Instead of saying, "What if this were real?" it dashes any expectation of verisimilitude in service of an almost twisted fantasy indicative of the contrived plot of a children's creepypasta. I do feel obliged to commend you for that — for going back and emulating the decade-and-a-half-old legacy of evoking unsettling images purely through text on a message board. But the stark contrast here, between after-dark forum post storytelling and actual creepypasta-tier violence in the "real world", is difficult to swallow.

I don't think the idea of cliché-creepypasta-turned-real is an unattainable narrative that can't function. In fact, I recognize it works immensely well, given the firestorm of popularity and interest surrounding this work. I just wish this article took the feeling of almost-realism and went beyond with it. I mean no insult when I say, I almost wish this article about a cliché creepypasta wasn't just like a cliché creepypasta — but, instead, a fleshed-out story. One which did not rely on edgy shock horror to sell its points. One which did not inject, at times, artificial remorse the reader should somehow feel for this character who is just as awful as the article presents. There needs to be something to offset all of this in a rich and fulfilling way.

– hide block

Forgive my rambling — I thank you for creating this article that makes me nostalgic of the creepy after-dark forums I browsed as a teen. And I admire what went into the multimedia presentation. But reading this carefully makes me question, how much stock should I put into it? What merit does this have, beyond all the feelings of nostalgia and novelty?

item.content:encoded:
While at first glance, there is a lot going for this article (the art, for instance, is very additive and interesting, and I enjoyed a fair bit of the forum dynamics), with closer scrutiny I didn't get too much out of this. There just seems like a lot of wasted potential here, as the base anomaly/quirk of this piece is an intriguing concept but was just not utilized to its best ability. For example, you could really make the long list about Michael murdering all of his bullies a lot scarier, but the dense, intentionally poorly written prose really makes a lot of the parts in this a lot less potent. I also found myself being kinda disappointed over how this just… fizzled out at the end.

All in all, I'm afraid to say this is a downvote.

item.title: Re: -1
item.content:encoded:
Very fair, but I must comment on your addendum because I can’t help but simply disagree with.

I wanted to write about how Parawatch would interact with a clearly anomalous entity, and I think in that regard, I succeeded. I actually do plan on writing a “blurry line between fiction and reality” sometime, so stay tuned for that! And the 666 stuff, yeah, it is corny and on the nose, but micheal isn’t an entity I would call subtle.

Thanks so much for the feedback, though, this is really helpful!!

I appreciate the effort, but I couldn't get into it. It was glaringly obvious where this was going as soon as rastamasta posted the thing, and the dialogue alternated between laughable and overexpositional on the part of nearly every single other poster in the thread. The post numbers also descending into repetitions of 6 was corny & on the nose, to put it lightly. The ending repeat was pretty good, as was the initial post - but everything in between (save for the images, nicely done on those) failed to capture the unsettling mood that it seemed to be going for.

As a small addendum, I find that this also lacks the verisimilitude that made other Parawatch pieces, particularly Hippo's initial one's like Sunday and Abwesenheit so fantastic. The unclear, blurry line between the fiction and the real accentuated by the manner of storytelling is entirely absent in this. Between the dialogue and the small unrealistic bits that pulled me out (the post numbers were a particularly egregious, if minor, example), I couldn't imagine — or, more importantly, feel like was this actually happening, which is essentially what Parawatch and, I daresay, all good classic creepypasta derive their horror and engagement from.
